papers.title: Unified scaling of transmon sub-resonant parametric drive strength limits
papers.abstract: Achieving fast gates and high-fidelity readout in superconducting quantum circuits often benefits from the use of large amplitude microwave drives. As the strength increases, unwanted effects such as excitation out of the logical states also become more prevalent. In transmon qubits, coherent controls relying on sub-resonant drives are fundamentally limited by the eventual appearance of strong hybridization in the spectrum. Understanding how this threshold depends on intrinsic device parameters is vital for the design and operation of circuits utilizing the transmon as a source of nonlinearity. In this work, we present an experimental study of 14 transmons with a wide range of anharmonicities, and use comparison with Floquet branch analysis and semiclassical simulations to establish a straightforward relationship between the critical value of the effective drive amplitude $η_{\max}$ and the ratio $γ=ω_q/α$, where $ω_q$ is the transmon frequency and $-α$ is the anharmonicity. For the case where the transmon is used as a parametrically driven coupler, these results further allow us to estimate maximum parametric interaction rates, which informs the circuit design process for optimizing gate rates and fidelities.

similar_to.title: Characterization of drive-induced unwanted state transitions in superconducting circuits

summary.summary: Measurements on 14 transmons with a wide range of anharmonicities show that the largest usable sub-resonant drive amplitude, above which the spectrum hybridizes strongly ('chaos') and the transmon leaves its logical states, is set by a single parameter, $\gamma = \omega_q/\alpha$. The threshold scales as $\eta_\mathrm{max} \propto \gamma^{0.61}$, with a prefactor that depends only weakly on the normalized drive frequency.
summary.motivation: Strong drives speed up gates and readout but eventually excite the transmon out of its logical states, and how that threshold depends on design parameters was not established. For a transmon used as a parametrically driven coupler the threshold caps the interaction rate, which is the product of the anharmonicity and $\eta_\mathrm{max}$.
summary.method: Each transmon ($\gamma$ from 18 to 99 in the examples shown) receives a sub-resonant stimulation pulse over a range of drive frequencies and amplitudes, and the remaining ground-state population is measured. The thresholds are compared with Floquet branch analysis and a semiclassical model.
summary.result: Experiment and the three threshold estimates agree across the drive-frequency range, with the largest deviations near nonlinear resonances, the strongest being the fourth-order 1:3 resonance. At $\eta_\mathrm{max}$ the Stark shift is about $\omega_q/8$ whatever the anharmonicity, so the only clear way to much faster parametric rates is a higher coupler frequency; rates are tabulated for a 5 GHz coupler with 150 MHz anharmonicity and $g/\Delta = 0.1$.

papers.title: Error Correction in a Distributed Quantum Computer
papers.abstract: Building fault-tolerant quantum computers with large numbers of logical qubits requires both scalable hardware architectures and error-correcting codes that make efficient use of physical qubits. Photonic interconnects address both of these challenges by allowing the physical qubits to be distributed across multiple processors while providing the non-local connectivity necessary to implement resource-efficient codes such as high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. A key requirement for realising this architecture is the ability to perform stabiliser measurements between remote processors, which has not previously been demonstrated experimentally. Here we report the first experimental demonstration of distributed quantum error detection and correction. We generate entanglement between network qubits in two separate trapped-ion processors and use it to perform remote syndrome measurements on data qubits. We first realise a distributed [[2, 1, 1]] repetition code, detecting phase-flip errors on a logical qubit encoded across the two modules in real time and suppressing logical errors. We then combine these mid-circuit syndrome measurements with real-time feedforward to actively correct arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a distributed Bell state. These results provide an experimental foundation for quantum error correction (QEC) across modular quantum architectures.

similar_to.title: Demonstration of High-Fidelity Entangled Logical Qubits using Transmons
High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory

summary.summary: This is the first experimental demonstration of distributed error detection and correction: stabilizers are measured across two trapped-ion modules about 2 m apart, using a photonically generated Bell pair between network qubits as a shared ancilla for the data qubits. A distributed $[[2,1,1]]$ repetition code detects phase flips in real time, and feedforward corrects arbitrary single-qubit Pauli errors on a Bell state shared between the modules.
summary.motivation: Photonic links would let physical qubits be spread over modules and supply the non-local connectivity that high-rate qLDPC codes need. Syndrome extraction between data qubits in different processors had not been shown experimentally.
summary.method: The network Bell pair allows the parity of the two remote data qubits to be read out with only local mixed-species ($^{88}\mathrm{Sr}^+$/$^{43}\mathrm{Ca}^+$) gates and classical communication. Phase-flip errors are injected with probability $p$ through random $Z$ rotations, and depolarizing noise of strength $\lambda$ is applied for the Bell-state test.
summary.result: At zero injected error the stabilizer measurement returns the target outcome with probability 96.4(6)%; conditioning on it keeps the logical qubit in the code space and lowers the logical error over the full range of $p$, and repeating it does not measurably raise the logical error rate. With correction the Bell-state fidelity stays roughly constant against $\lambda$ (the prepared state is 82.5(15)%), limited mainly by the local mixed-species gates, and sympathetic recooling adds 2.2 ms per round, cutting the entanglement rate from about 100/s to 10/s.

papers.title: Factoring six-digit integers with superconducting quantum circuits
papers.abstract: Integer factorization is a central computational problem with important applications in public-key cryptography. Here, we demonstrate a quantum factorization protocol using a superconducting circuit. Microwave drives are used to engineer a highly tunable effective two-level Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues can be measured spectroscopically. The target integer \(N\) and each candidate factor pair (\(p\),\(q\)) are encoded into the amplitudes, frequencies, and phases of the applied microwave fields. By scanning the candidate pairs while monitoring the spectral response at zero energy, we identify the factor pairs of integers up to six digits. The protocol requires neither two-qubit gates nor quantum entanglement. Its performance is currently limited by the precision of microwave control and the finite linewidth of the spectroscopic response. Improved control accuracy and longer coherence times would extend the accessible range of integers.

similar_to.title: Experimental realization of an intrinsically error-protected superconducting qubit

summary.summary: A superconducting transmon coupled to a cavity implements single-qubit factorization by encoding integers $N$ and candidate factors $(p,q)$ into an effective two-level Hamiltonian via microwave drives, then identifying factor pairs by spectroscopic detection of zero eigenvalues. The protocol successfully factors six-digit integers such as $N=113569$ (factors $337 \times 337$) without requiring two-qubit gates or entanglement.
summary.motivation: Current quantum implementations of Shor's algorithm rely on high-fidelity multi-qubit gates that remain experimentally challenging; a single-qubit approach using direct Hamiltonian engineering could circumvent these obstacles.
summary.method: Microwave drives with tunable amplitudes, frequencies, and phases engineer the effective magnetic field components $B_0$, $B_1$, $B_3$ of a two-level Hamiltonian. Integer $N$ is encoded in the off-diagonal element, candidate pair $(p,q)$ in the diagonal elements. A construct drive controls the $\{|\uparrow\rangle,|\downarrow\rangle\}$ subspace (derived from transmon levels $|2\rangle,|3\rangle$), and an offset drive tunes the $\{|0\rangle,|1\rangle\}$ subspace to set the zero-energy reference. Spectroscopic readout measures the excited-state population at zero energy; peaks identify factor pairs satisfying $pq=N$.
summary.result: For $N=113569$, the protocol identifies $(p,q)=(337,337)$ via spectroscopic screening of candidate pairs, with classical verification of selected peaks. Current performance is limited by microwave control precision ($\approx 1\%$ amplitude noise, $\approx 50$ kHz uncertainty at $\Omega_0/2\pi=5$ MHz) and transmon coherence ($T_2^* \approx 5$ μs, linewidth $\sim 30$ kHz). Numerical simulations show that improving to $\Omega_0/2\pi=50$ MHz and $T_2=100$ μs would reduce candidate pairs requiring verification by approximately two orders of magnitude.

papers.title: Security Implications of Measurement Based Crosstalk on Superconducting Quantum Computers
papers.abstract: Crosstalk is one of the major issues for scalability of superconducting quantum processors. But it can also be used by threat actors to intentionally sabotage computations and steal information. This paper analyzes data leakage due to crosstalk during qubit measurement. Prior research yielded an accuracy of 96% in classifying measurement of one qubit in IBM quantum computers. When evaluated on superconducting hardware from VTT, we achieved an accuracy of 71.68% with similar framework. Our extended framework with additional labels yields an accuracy of 76.30% for classifying measurement of one qubit and 53.37% for measurement of two qubits using Support Vector Machine (SVM). Experimental results indicate that measurement operation on a qubit can affect the probability of measuring adjacent qubits. The impact on the target qubit is dependent on the number of neighboring qubits measured and also the measurement outcome.

similar_to.title: System Characterization of Dispersive Readout in Superconducting Qubits

summary.summary: This work demonstrates that measurement-induced crosstalk on superconducting quantum processors can leak information about victim qubits to adjacent attacker qubits, enabling potential side-channel attacks. Using Support Vector Machine classifiers on VTT Q50 hardware, the authors achieve 76.30% accuracy for single-victim classification and 53.37% for two-victim scenarios, showing hardware-dependent vulnerability compared to prior IBM work (96% accuracy).
summary.motivation: Measurement crosstalk is a known scalability issue in superconducting quantum processors, but its potential exploitation as a security threat in multi-tenant cloud quantum systems has not been thoroughly evaluated across different hardware platforms.
summary.method: Circuits with 1–10 $X$ gates applied to victim qubits (Q0, Q2) were executed on VTT Q50 (53-qubit superconducting processor with lattice topology), measuring the probability of the attacker qubit reading $|1\rangle$ across configurations: single victim measured as $|0\rangle$, $|1\rangle$, or not measured (two-qubit case); two victims with six measurement combinations (three-qubit case). RBF SVM classifiers were trained on 900–1800 circuits at 1000 shots each.
summary.result: Two-qubit framework achieved 76.30% accuracy (precision 0.7724, recall 0.7553) with additional measurement scenarios versus prior work; three-qubit framework yielded 53.37% accuracy; measurement-count framework (ignoring outcome, only counting measured qubits) achieved 86.11% accuracy, showing impact scales with number of simultaneously measured neighbors.
